evidence_items.claim: Pauline letters identify a major collection for Jerusalem; Acts narrates the journey and delegates but does not foreground the money, creating a debated omission.
The apostolic decree has important textual variants, including shorter moralized forms in Western witnesses, so wording and purpose require textual-critical control.
The porneia item in Acts 15 has competing explanations involving broad sexual wrongdoing, prohibited kinship unions, Leviticus 17-18 resident-alien rules, Noachide rules, and table fellowship.

evidence_items.claim: Historical evaluation of Acts must compare particular claims with independent evidence rather than assign blanket reliability or unreliability.
Acts is preserved in early papyri and major Greek codices, with P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae contributing different portions and textual profiles.
First-person plural sections occur in Acts 16, 20-21, and 27-28, but their source and implication for authorship remain disputed.
Codex Bezae and related versional witnesses preserve a substantially distinctive text of Acts often called Western, whose individual readings require case-by-case judgment.
Acts presents women as disciples, prophets, patrons, hosts, household leaders, teachers, workers, converts, and sufferers, though narration remains selective and patriarchal constraints persist.
The dominant form names idols, sexual immorality, strangled material, and blood; Codex Bezae omits the strangled item and adds negative reciprocity.

relevance_metadata.parent_title: Second Temple Priesthood and Temple Authority

evidence_items.claim: The operative setting is Roman-period Jerusalem. The inscription is direct evidence for a locally enforced sacred-space boundary and should not be replaced with generic claims about ancient inscriptions or imperial administration.
The warning materializes graded holiness and restricted access within the temple complex while using Greek to address visitors who might not read Hebrew or Aramaic.

The complete stone was found in Jerusalem in 1871 and is held by the Istanbul Archaeology Museums as 2196 T; a fragmentary parallel is held by the Israel Museum. The warning belongs to the Herodian temple horizon before its destruction in 70 CE.
Herodian temple complex in Jerusalem, approximately 23 BCE-70 CE.
Greek-reading visitors approaching restricted areas of the Jerusalem temple complex.
The inscription and Josephus independently describe a boundary separating areas open to foreigners from the more restricted sanctuary precinct.
